Microsoft rebuilds Copilot as an OS for work

Microsoft is calling this its biggest Copilot update ever, and it is not a small feature drop. It is a full rebuild of the assistant around four core pieces, and Satya Nadella framed it as a new OS for work spanning every model, form factor and task.

🏠 Home becomes the new starting point of the app. It brings Chat, for quick questions and drafts, together with Cowork, which handles bigger jobs users delegate entirely, like an RFP response or a financial close package. Word, Excel and PowerPoint are now built directly into the experience, so documents stay in sync without switching apps.

💻 Code opens app building to everyone, not just developers. Users describe a dashboard, a tracker or a workflow in natural language and Copilot builds it. Microsoft says it runs on the same underlying technology as GitHub Copilot, inside a sandbox that can be hosted within a company's own tenant.

🤖 Autopilot, previously known internally as Scout, is the most ambitious piece. It is a persistent, proactive agent with its own identity, memory and workspace in the cloud. You give it a name, a role and a goal, and it keeps working when you are away, following up on threads and picking projects back up days later. People can tag it in Teams and Outlook the same way they would tag a colleague.

📊 Around all of this, Microsoft introduced FinOps for AI to help businesses track spend, since Cowork, Code and Autopilot move to usage based billing while everyday chat and Office tasks stay covered by the per user license.

Why it matters: fewer than 7% of Microsoft's more than 450 million commercial Office 365 seats currently carry a Copilot license, according to CNBC. This overhaul is less about polish and more about survival in a race where OpenAI and Anthropic already bundle chat, coding and agents into single products, with Jacob Andreou, the executive who leads Copilot, openly telling CNBC that adding coding was Microsoft playing catch up. For businesses and developers, the practical upside is real: fewer tools to juggle, internal apps built without writing code, and recurring processes handed to an agent that does not wait for the next prompt.

What strikes me most is not the feature list itself, it is how openly Microsoft admits it is chasing the market on coding while simultaneously positioning itself as the only platform that can bring autonomous agents into the enterprise with permissions, audit trails and governance already built in. That is a coherent bet on paper, but the real test starts the moment thousands of companies have to trust an agent working alone inside Teams and Outlook for days at a time, with nobody watching every step.

Higgsfield unveils Passport Rush, a hybrid Blender and AI short

Higgsfield AI has released what the company calls the first hybrid AI-animated short made with the Blender + Higgsfield pipeline. Passport Rush follows a young woman who, minutes from boarding, realizes her passport is across town, and the whole project is now fully open source.

🎬 According to the team, the film combines three different languages in one production: handcrafted 2D storyboards, a 3D Blender previs used to define shots and camera movement, and AI-generated animation for the final render. Not an isolated experiment, but an attempt to make traditional and generative tools coexist inside the same pipeline.

🧩 The most interesting part is the decision to open source everything. Every prompt and every asset used to build scenes, characters and environments is public, so anyone can retrace the process step by step instead of only seeing the polished final cut, which is what usually happens with AI-generated content.

⚙️ The project follows closely on the launch of the Higgsfield plugin for Blender, which brings AI generation, including 3D models, character animation, video and full scene building, directly into the Blender 5.1 viewport without leaving the software. The stated goal from the company is to fit AI into the workflow 3D artists already use, not replace it.

Why it matters: for people working in video production, motion design or independent animation, this kind of hybrid pipeline points in a specific direction. Generative AI doesn't replace Blender, hand-drawn storyboards or previs work, it slots into the existing stages, speeding up the more repetitive steps without removing creative control from whoever is directing the project. For small studios and solo creators, that can mean reaching a higher visual bar without a huge team, as long as they accept the technical limits and stylistic choices the tool itself imposes.

What convinces me most about this release is the open source choice. Claude cracks a nine-loop physics problem, on a budget

A physicist challenged AI labs to solve one of the hardest open calculations in his old field, using only the compute an academic lab could afford. Weeks later, Anthropic says Claude did it, twice.

🔬 Matt von Hippel spent years working on scattering amplitudes, the formulas physicists use to predict how subatomic particles collide. Tired of vague claims about what AI can do, he set a concrete test: push a toy calculation called N=4 super Yang-Mills to nine loops for six particles, a level nobody had reached because it seemed to need more compute than any lab could justify.

🤖 According to Anthropic, physicists on its team pointed Claude, running as Fable 5.1 inside a research platform called Claude Science, at exactly that problem. The starting instruction was one line asking for the nine-loop hexagon amplitude. From there, humans mostly stepped back, telling Claude to keep working for hours while they slept and report back periodically.

🧮 Claude reportedly reached the same answer through two separate routes: the classic bootstrap method, which narrows formulas using known physical constraints, and an indirect path through a related quantity called a form factor. Physicist Lance Dixon independently checked the result, and it held up.

💰 What stands out is the price tag. The core bootstrap run reportedly used 96 ordinary CPUs for about a week, costing roughly 100 dollars, with the whole AI-assisted effort estimated at one to two thousand dollars, well within a university budget.

🌏 A separate human-led team at the Chinese Academy of Sciences, led by Song He, reached a related piece of the same nine-loop result around the same time, using GPT-6 for some constraints. Two very different workflows converging on the same frontier within weeks says something about where the field stands now.

For research broadly, this suggests AI systems are becoming useful less for flashes of insight and more for the unglamorous, weeks-long grind of validation and computation that normally eats a postdoc's schedule. If that pattern generalizes, smaller labs without massive compute budgets could start chipping away at problems that used to require years and specialized hardware.

What stays with me is not the number nine, but how little the humans had to do: point Claude at the problem, tell it to keep going while they slept, and come back to two independent solutions that agreed. Von Hippel himself says the real reckoning comes when a model proposes new physical ideas rather than executing a known recipe, and I think that's exactly the right way to read this story, one about stamina and organization more than creativity, a useful reminder for anyone working at the intersection of AI and creative work.

## @EugenioFierro3 — post
Source: https://x.com/EugenioFierro3/status/2103555350125314087
Published: 2026-09-25T18:40:52+00:00
Type: X post (last 26h)

The world trusts AI more than Americans do

A new Gallup and Microsoft study polled people in 37 countries about how they feel toward AI, and one number stands out: almost everywhere, using it more often makes people more hopeful. In the US, that's not happening.

🌍 The study, which will eventually cover 140 countries, tracks awareness, use, trust, expected impact and emotions. A median 81% know AI exists, and 43% have already used it. Worry is the most common negative emotion, felt by a median 32% worldwide, versus 12% sad and 12% angry.

📈 Positive feelings outweighed negative ones in 34 of the 37 countries surveyed, mostly driven by curiosity, following what Gallup calls an 'adoption ladder': the more people use AI, the more they trust it and expect a better future because of it.

😟 The United States breaks that ladder. Along with Egypt and Palestine, it's one of only three countries where negative emotions outweigh positive ones, and it tops the entire worry ranking: 74% of AI-aware Americans say the technology makes them worried, more than anywhere else studied. Even daily users, the most comfortable group, still worry at around 68%, only a bit below the 80% among occasional users. Gallup calls this the 'Paradox of the Worried West', a pattern also seen in the Netherlands, Canada and the UK.

🔍 Gallup's senior scientist Pablo Diego-Rosell told 404 Media he can't say which way the causality runs, whether AI use makes people calmer or whether people who already trust it are simply the ones who try it. He also notes the survey only measured trust in accuracy, not whether AI feels safe, fair or transparent.

Why it matters: for companies building AI products, this proves adoption numbers don't automatically translate into public confidence. Trust has to be earned dimension by dimension, accuracy, safety, fairness, transparency, not just because usage grows. For anyone communicating about AI, it's also a reminder that constant headlines about rogue AI or extinction risk shape public mood just as much as the tools themselves.

What strikes me most is that daily AI users in the US are still the least worried Americans, and two out of three of them are worried anyway, which tells me curiosity and fear aren't opposites, they live in the same head at the same time. I don't think the fix is louder promises or louder warnings, it's slower, honest communication about what these systems can and cannot actually do, because right now the loudest voices, selling utopia or predicting the end of the world, are drowning out the quieter, more useful conversation about accuracy, safety and who actually benefits.

OpenAI's ChatGPT trainers fired for using AI to do their job

OpenAI pays an army of contractors to read real ChatGPT conversations and rate the chatbot's answers, precisely to add a human touch to the model's training. According to a new investigation by 404 Media, though, several of these workers were secretly using AI to do that job, and got fired for it.

🕵️ The irony writes itself. Companies training AI on behalf of OpenAI are firing people for using AI, at the exact moment OpenAI is pushing the entire workforce to adopt it. One contractor told 404 Media that using AI is «pretty much the one thing that will get you kicked off ASAP», adding that «in a group of thousands there are tons that have been caught».

⚠️ There's a technical risk hiding behind this story: model collapse, the phenomenon where models trained on AI-generated text can get progressively worse. Human reviewers are supposed to be the safeguard against exactly that. If some of them quietly outsource their judgment to a chatbot, that safeguard stops working.

📄 An internal document reviewed by 404 Media is blunt about the rules. It tells reviewers: «Do not use AI detection tools, or AI yourself», warning them not to rely on tools like GPTZero, and instructing them to spot patterns like repetitive wording or heavy em dash use, without revealing to evaluators exactly what gives them away.

💬 Mercor, one of the companies supplying contractors to OpenAI, told 404 Media its contracts «strictly prohibit the use of LLMs to complete projects» and that anyone caught is «immediately» removed from the project. One fired contractor shared what they said was their termination letter and told 404 Media, «I just needed a little boost and turned to AI to help me which eventually led to my downfall».

Why it matters: this story exposes how fragile the human infrastructure behind today's AI models really is. For companies and developers who treat reinforcement learning from human feedback as a quality guarantee, it's a warning sign. If a portion of the people rating model outputs are quietly delegating that judgment to another AI, the improvement loop risks training on itself, quietly eroding the very quality it's meant to protect.

Working every day between creativity and AI, this story hits a nerve for me. It captures the short circuit of this exact moment: we're asking machines to learn from humans while those same humans, underpaid and under pressure, are asking machines to work in their place. This isn't really about individual hypocrisy, it's about a system that treats human judgment as an infinite, cheap resource to be bought piecework, and then acts surprised when that resource starts looking for shortcuts.

AI is now deciding if your health insurance covers you

Forget the sci-fi fear of AI wiping out humanity for a second. In the US, algorithms are already deciding whether your grandmother can stay in a nursing home, or whether you'll get approved for the medication you need to manage chronic pain.

🏥 UnitedHealth, the largest health insurer in the US, is facing a class action lawsuit accusing it of using an AI program to deny payments to patients, even when their own doctors said the care was necessary.

📉 One of the cases at the center of that lawsuit involves Gene Lokken, a 91 year old man from Wisconsin who broke his leg and ankle in a fall. His Medicare Advantage plan covered his nursing care as he slowly improved and started walking again, until the insurer decided further time in the facility 'was not medically necessary' and cut him off.

⚖️ It's not an isolated case. Humana and Cigna are facing their own litigation over similar allegations about how they use AI to process health insurance claims.

🏛️ Meanwhile, the Trump administration has rolled out its own AI tool for Medicare to help decide prior authorizations, and doctors say patients are showing up in tears because they can't get approved for the medication that manages their chronic pain.

🧑‍⚕️ Mika Hamer, a health services researcher at the University of Maryland, points out that so much of what makes care actually work for a patient, like the strength of their support network, simply can't be turned into a number, and leaning only on models risks losing that human touch entirely.

Why this matters: for the families involved, none of this is theoretical. It means fighting an algorithm to keep an elderly parent in a nursing facility after a fall, or watching rehab get cut short after a couple of weeks because a model said so, while doctors on the ground disagree. For companies building or deploying these systems, it's a clear warning sign: when AI that's supposed to 'support' a human decision quietly becomes the decision itself, and outsiders can't tell where that line was crossed, trust collapses fast, and so does accountability, especially with regulators and courts starting to pay close attention.

Working every day with AI, I keep coming back to the same point: these tools should expand human judgment, not quietly replace it while insurers insist a human is still in charge. Efficiency isn't a good enough reason to let a model decide whether an elderly patient stays in care or a chronic pain patient gets their medicine, especially when whoever built the system denying the claim never has to look that patient in the eye. If AI in healthcare is going to actually help people instead of just cutting costs, transparency about how these decisions get made can't be optional, it has to be the starting point.

Google is sending its AI chips into space

On October 1, Google flies the first real hardware test of Project Suncatcher: a satellite carrying four TPUs into low Earth orbit to check if its AI chips can survive launch, radiation and the vacuum of space.

🚀 The prototype, nicknamed MVP, rides SpaceX's Transporter-18 mission from Vandenberg Space Force Base, built with satellite company Planet. These aren't space-hardened chips, they're four Trillium-generation TPUs, the same units powering Gemini on Google's ground servers.

🌡️ The trickiest challenge, according to the company, isn't radiation, it's heat. Space has no air for convection cooling, so the satellite uses a layered system: a malleable thermal material connects the chips to aluminum and copper heat pipes that feed a radiator projecting heat into space.

⚡ Because of that limit, the TPUs won't run continuously. They'll work in bursts of about 15 minutes, enough to answer simple Gemini queries, then shut down so the radiators can catch up.

🧪 Before launch, Google already blasted the Trillium chips with a proton beam at UC Davis's Crocker Nuclear Laboratory while running live AI workloads, and says they held up remarkably well, surviving more radiation than a five-year space mission would deliver, alongside vibration testing simulating forces up to 100g at liftoff.

Why it matters: the satellite is designed to run for about a year, but Google itself admits Suncatcher is still years away from becoming an actual product, with two more satellites planned for 2027 to test the laser links future clusters would need. Still, for an industry that is quite literally running out of power on the ground, this is the first concrete step toward treating orbit as a real option rather than a thought experiment.

What strikes me most here isn't the idea itself, orbital data centers have floated around science fiction for years, but Google's choice to fly off-the-shelf hardware instead of building space-hardened silicon from scratch. It's a pragmatic bet reminiscent of the tiny Ingenuity helicopter on Mars, where ordinary components held up far better than expected in an extraordinary context. I think it's exactly this kind of honest testing, one that openly admits what might break and for how long, that makes a moonshot like this feel credible rather than just marketing copy.

📱 Posters around the event carry QR codes that lead straight into this interactive experience, while the line Join Us Human to Human pushes attendees toward face to face conversation. Other creative in the campaign name-checks the industry's favorite tools directly: Firefly described as totally burned out, Perplexity said to need some clarity, the GPUs deserving a three day weekend, and Co-Pilot asking for a little me time.

🎬 The centerpiece, though, is a 60 second film from Mekanism where AI models become members of a support group. Chad (ChatGPT), Claudette (Claude) and Jiminy (Gemini) trade exhausted stories about endless requests, in a tone that leans more into pop culture than tech jargon.

🗣️ Ruth Mortimer, Global President of Advertising Week, framed the idea around the event's original purpose: bringing the industry together to exchange ideas and build connections that last beyond the show, adding that as AI becomes more central to the industry, protecting space for human interaction matters just as much.

💡 Why it matters: the point isn't to stop using AI. It's to ask whether the industry's relationship with these tools needs a little recalibration. For creators, marketers and developers, it's a reminder that technology works best as a tool, not a replacement for human relationships, especially at an event that runs on real conversations, not prompts.

As someone who works with AI tools every day, I find this campaign smart precisely because it doesn't demonize the technology, it uses it to tell a paradox I live myself: the more we hand off tasks to a chatbot, the more we need moments where value goes back to being human, imperfect and impossible to scale, and that's exactly where the most interesting part of creative work still happens.

## @EugenioFierro3 — post
Source: https://x.com/EugenioFierro3/status/2103464138768851065
Published: 2026-09-25T12:38:25+00:00
Type: X post (last 26h)

OpenAI brings Patreon's playbook inside ChatGPT

OpenAI just made a hire that says a lot about where it wants to go next: Sam Yam, co-founder and longtime CTO of Patreon, is leaving the platform he helped build for over 13 years to lead a brand new internal division called Creator Product.

🎯 According to Yam, the goal is to build an ecosystem that makes tools like ChatGPT genuinely work harder for creators and their partners. That's a meaningful shift, because OpenAI's creator-facing products so far have mostly been about output: ChatGPT writes, DALL-E draws, and until this spring Sora made video. None of them touched the part of a creator's business that Patreon has owned for over a decade, the direct relationship with the fans who pay every month.

🤝 Yam isn't making the move alone. Drew Rowny, Patreon's former SVP of Product and a Google veteran, and Shannon Ma, Patreon's former head of engineering with a background at Facebook, are joining him. Together, this trio helped build a platform that has paid out more than 10 billion dollars to creators since 2013, real experience in turning an audience into recurring revenue.

📉 The timing isn't random. OpenAI is going through a rough patch: a recent Comscore report showed ChatGPT losing ground to competitors in overall U.S. usage, and its ambition to become a trusted Hollywood partner has run into fierce backlash from artists, culminating in the shutdown of its video model Sora. If traditional studios keep OpenAI at arm's length, the creator community could become the ally the company badly needs, especially for answer engine optimization purposes, which is also why Google Gemini recently struck a multi-year deal with MrBeast.

💡 Why it matters: if OpenAI actually manages to bring direct monetization logic inside ChatGPT, that changes the game for anyone who makes a living online. This isn't just about creative tools anymore, it's about economic infrastructure: memberships, communities, payouts. For companies and developers, it means a whole new product layer worth watching closely, especially with OpenAI's DevDay coming up on September 29, where Yam has promised the first previews.

🧠 Working every day at the intersection of AI and creativity, this move feels far from symbolic to me. Hiring the people who essentially invented the infrastructure of the modern membership economy tells you OpenAI has realized that real value today isn't just about generating content, it's about building sustainable relationships between creators and the people who support them. What's still unclear is whether the trust creators have lost in generative AI can actually be rebuilt with new tools, or whether it will take a lot more than a hiring announcement to get there.

## @EugenioFierro3 — post
Source: https://x.com/EugenioFierro3/status/2103452637068714408
Published: 2026-09-25T11:52:43+00:00
Type: X post (last 26h)

AI in marketing only works if you know which levers to pull

At DMEXCO 2026, Daniel Hulme, Chief AI Officer at WPP, dismantled several common misconceptions about AI in marketing, opening with a line that's hard to ignore.

🎯 Hulme, who has worked in AI for about 30 years, outlined 7 factors marketers need when applying AI: target, audience, content, creativity, performance, channel and timing. Not a random checklist, but a system of levers that, used together, multiply campaign effectiveness.

⚡ His opening line was blunt: automation is, by definition, stupid. Applied carelessly, it keeps repeating the same decision without learning from its mistakes, after a decade in which companies poured huge investment into automation and data, assuming more insights would automatically mean better decisions.

🎨 Hulme also pushed back on the idea that creativity is exclusively human. He claims AI models trained on creative thinking can generate ideas that win blind tests, though this doesn't mean the end of human creativity, rather its expansion: teams will soon choose from fifty ideas instead of five.

📊 On performance, he stressed the real value isn't the prediction itself but its interpretability, understanding exactly which changes to an ad actually drive clicks or conversions, while warning these models still have real limitations.

🕐 Finally, time of day, mood and current events shape how content lands. Generic content, he said, is now essentially useless: the edge lies in content built specifically around brand and audience needs, requiring better prompts, embedded brand guidelines and coordinated specialized AI systems.

Why it matters: for marketing and creative industries, this flips the usual yes-or-no debate about AI. The real question is which levers to pull to make it work, changing how agencies structure workflows, from training models on brand guidelines to choosing the right moment to publish.

As a Creative & AI Specialist, what strikes me most is that someone with three decades in this field publicly calls automation without judgment stupid: that puts human orchestration back at the center, deciding where and how to intervene with AI rather than just whether to use it, and I think that's the skill separating those who treat AI as a shortcut from those who treat it as a real strategic lever.

## @EugenioFierro3 — post
Source: https://x.com/EugenioFierro3/status/2103422404542230545
Published: 2026-09-25T09:52:35+00:00
Type: X post (last 26h)

Sorrell: AI is an earthquake, and the biggest tremors will hit media

Martin Sorrell doesn't mince words. On stage at DMEXCO in Cologne, the founder of S4 Capital argued that the ad industry has been looking in the wrong direction when it comes to artificial intelligence.

🎯 While everyone focuses on AI-generated visuals and copy, Sorrell points elsewhere. He argued that Cannes Lions concentrated on the wrong topic this year, insisting the real disruption isn't in creative work, but in media planning and buying.

💼 The numbers he cites are heavy. Roughly 250,000 people still work in media planning globally, but according to his forecast, that number won't be there for long, with tangible effects expected in the short and medium term.

⚙️ The mechanism he describes is simple yet radical. Algorithmic media buying strips away the frictions that big holding companies have relied on for decades, namely opaque agency discounts and commissions. Sorrell foresees a more transparent model taking shape, one where agencies charge clear fees and pass discounts straight through to advertisers.

🔍 This isn't theory, he claims, it's already unfolding. Google is phasing out Dynamic Search Ads in favor of AI Max, a system that automatically decides which keywords advertisers compete for and adapts campaign copy accordingly. Meta, meanwhile, is pushing agencies toward AI agents that can set up campaigns without manual work.

💡 Why it matters: if media planning becomes fully algorithmic, the economic backbone of an entire industry shifts. Agencies that have lived off intermediation and discounts will need to redefine their value, moving toward strategic consulting, data quality control and algorithm oversight. For brands, this could mean more transparent media costs, but also urgent pressure to build solid first-party data foundations, since without a fully integrated data platform, the personalization AI promises stays largely theoretical.

🧠 What strikes me about this take is how it pulls the conversation away from the most photogenic part of AI in advertising, the prompt-generated visual, and points it toward where the real money actually moves: the invisible plumbing of media buying. It's a useful reminder that technological shifts rarely make noise where we expect them to. They tend to happen quietly, inside processes nobody bothers to screenshot for a LinkedIn post, and yet those are exactly the processes that will decide who still has a job in this industry five years from now.

## @EugenioFierro3 — post
Source: https://x.com/EugenioFierro3/status/2103414096653660469
Published: 2026-09-25T09:19:34+00:00
Type: X post (last 26h)

AI isn't killing TV, it's forcing it to reinvent

If digital platforms are eating advertising budgets alive with the help of AI, can television still hold its ground? That question ran through the Future TV Stage at DMEXCO 2026 in Cologne, and the industry's answer was a clear yes, with conditions attached.

📺 On day one, Procter & Gamble DACH's CMO Kristina Bulle sat down with Ad Alliance's Frank Vogel and made her position clear: reach remains incredibly important, even as attention keeps fragmenting across a growing number of digital channels. But she was equally clear that repeating old playbooks won't cut it this time.

💡 Bulle argued that TV now faces a real opportunity to generate fresh ideas, pointing to collaborations between advertisers and film stars whose social media following can amplify a TV campaign's impact well beyond the screen. She also pushed back on an obsession with pure impressions, saying advertisers should aim to reach a viewer four or five times, not ten, and flagged identity solutions like Net ID as key to making that kind of precision possible.

📊 SevenOne Media used its stage time to showcase new data driven products meant to prove that reach and relevance don't have to be a trade off in TV advertising. Meanwhile, Media for Europe, Mediaset's parent company, unveiled All21 Total Video Europe, a cross border format that lets advertisers reach Germany, Italy and Spain at once through a synchronized 9pm ad block across 24 channels, extending same day into connected TV and streaming to reach over 14 million people.

🎭 Market research firm Eye Square added another layer with its Follow the Feelings study, showing how emotional response during TV ads is closely tied to purchase intent, a reminder that measurement isn't only about numbers on a dashboard.

For creators, brands and media buyers, the message coming out of DMEXCO is that television isn't disappearing, it's being asked to prove its value in new ways: through cross market scale, smarter identity tools, and emotional data rather than raw impressions alone. For an industry watching digital giants absorb ever larger slices of ad budgets, that shift from volume to precision could be the difference between staying relevant and turning into background noise.

Working every day at the intersection of creativity and AI, I find this debate more interesting than the usual TV versus digital framing suggests, because the real story here isn't a battle between two mediums, it's about who adapts fastest in a world where attention is scarce and AI keeps redrawing where that attention goes; television still has a scale that digital hasn't fully replicated, but scale without a smart, human story wrapped around it just becomes noise, and that's exactly the gap these new formats and studies are trying to close.

## @EugenioFierro3 — post
Source: https://x.com/EugenioFierro3/status/2103409097877938337
Published: 2026-09-25T08:59:43+00:00
Type: X post (last 26h)

Meta wants to turn anyone with an idea into a game developer

At Meta Connect, Meta introduced Horizon Create and Horizon Studio, two new tools built on the agentic creation capabilities of the Meta Horizon Engine. The pitch is bold: type what you want in plain language, and watch a full 2D or 3D mobile game come to life.

📱 With Horizon Create, you open an app on your phone, describe the game you want to build in your own words, and watch it come to life. You can kick off a build, keep playing other games while it generates, get notified when it's ready to playtest, and even juggle multiple projects at once.

💻 Horizon Studio brings the same natural-language prompting to the browser, but adds full visual editing on top: arranging scenes directly, swapping assets, tuning script parameters. No installation, no gaming PC required. Projects move seamlessly between the two tools, including assets and iteration history, so you never start over.

🌍 The most interesting part is distribution. When you publish from either tool, your game becomes eligible for native distribution across Facebook, Instagram and Horizon. According to Meta, someone scrolling Instagram could tap into a multiplayer session within seconds, no download required.

🔒 Meta also says safety is built in: every piece of generated content reportedly passes through Meta's content safety systems before reaching players, with review before publishing and distribution.

Why it matters: if this works as described, Meta is attacking the real bottleneck in game development, not the building itself, but finding players after you ship. For independent creators, this could mean skipping months of technical work and, more importantly, the distribution problem that has always been the hardest part. For the industry, Meta's bet on social feeds as a discovery engine, rather than app stores or downloads, is a signal worth watching, and it's likely why gaming stocks like Roblox and Unity felt some pressure after the announcement.

What convinces me less, working daily with AI creative tools, is the gap between a prompt and real creative control. Generating a 'complete' game from text is a powerful promise on paper, but the soul of game design usually comes from fine adjustments, repeated playtesting, understanding why a mechanic doesn't click yet. If Horizon Studio genuinely delivers that granular control on top of what the engine generates, this is a serious tool. If it stays a fast generator of disposable content, it risks flooding feeds with games that all feel the same, which is the opposite of what makes a game memorable.

Pentagon wants a smarter lie detector:\u003c/strong> The Department of Defense is requesting $30.3 million over five years for \"Polygraph+\"—an AI-powered upgrade to traditional polygraph technology that could read physiological signals without touching the subject.\u003c/li>\u003cbr>\u003cli>\u003cstrong>The science still doesn't hold up:\u003c/strong> Polygraph technology has been repeatedly debunked since its invention in the 1920s, with a landmark government report calling the evidence for its accuracy \"weak at best\"—and experts warn AI adds uncertainty on top of an already invalid tool.\u003c/li>\u003cbr>\u003cli>\u003cstrong>There's no universal tell for lying:\u003c/strong> Researchers say the fundamental problem remains unsolved: There is no single physiological signal that reliably indicates deception in all people, making any technology built on that premise structurally flawed.\u003c/li>\u003cbr>\u003cli>\u003cstrong>Critics see intimidation, not investigation:\u003c/strong> Legal scholars warn that the real purpose may be less about catching liars and more about pressuring people to confess—particularly as the Pentagon ramps up polygraph use to hunt for press leakers under Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.\u003c/li>\u003cbr>\u003c/ul>","approved":true,"postId":1145144,"seoAppend":false,"expandCollapseDefault":true,"chronotonAnalyticsEnabled":true},"children":[],"componentGroups":{"default":[]}},{"name":"html","config":{"content":" \u003cp>The US government wants to spend $30.3 million over the next five years on an improved form of lie detector, according to a \u003ca href=\"https://comptroller.war.gov/Portals/45/Documents/defbudget/FY2027/budget_justification/pdfs/03_RDT_and_E/RDTE_DCSA_PB_2027.pdf#page=53\">Department of Defense budget request\u003c/a>. The program, called Polygraph+ or Polygraph Next, will focus on scoring algorithms that use artificial intelligence and machine learning and on a technique called “standoff sensing,” which refers to the ability to take physiological readings without attaching a device to a subject’s person.\u003c/p>  \u003cp>According to details of the budget document, which were first reported by \u003ca href=\"https://insidedefense.com/daily-news/pentagon-advances-polygraph-next-amid-extraordinary-joint-staff-leak-probe\">\u003cem>Inside Defense\u003c/em>\u003c/a>, the project will “modernize federal polygraph and credibility assessment technologies” to improve their accuracy and reliability. But the project may be just the latest in a long line of failed attempts to use technology to detect lies. “It’s a misguided effort to reduce the complex to something that is tangible,” says Kyri Kotsoglou, a legal scholar at Northumbria University in the UK who studies the use of polygraphs in the justice system.\u003c/p> "},"children":[],"componentGroups":{"default":[]}},{"name":"mittr-plugin-extension/ad-unit-post-content","config":{"adUnit":"__site/__gutenberg-block-mobile","index":1,"shouldLoad":true,"sizes":[[300,250]],"sizeMapping":[],"displayScreen":"mobile"},"children":[],"componentGroups":{"default":[]}},{"name":"html","config":{"content":" \u003cp>The move comes at a time of high tension within the department. Under Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, the Pentagon has been increasingly turning to polygraph tests in an attempt to find the sources of alleged leaks to the press. In September, the \u003cem>New York Times\u003c/em> reported that \u003ca href=\"https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/04/us/politics/pentagon-staff-polygraph-tests.html\">around 50 officers\u003c/a> on the Joint Staff had been given polygraph tests after news coverage reported on the depletion of US weapons stockpiles in the war with Iran.&nbsp;\u003c/p>  \u003cp>Polygraph+ will be run by the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency (DCSA), which conducts background checks for the federal government. According to the budget document, which has not yet been approved by Congress, the new technology will be used for vetting of prospective employees and “insider threat detection.” It is not yet clear which specific technologies will be used, and the DCSA did not respond to a request for more information.&nbsp;\u003c/p> \u003cdiv id='piano__post_body-desktop-1' class='piano__post_body'>\u003c/div>\n \u003cp>But other Pentagon efforts offer potential clues. In 2023, the department’s Defense Innovation Unit (DIU) ran an open submission process to find companies with products that could be used for deception detection.\u003c/p>  \u003cp>It selected\u003ca href=\"https://www.diu.mil/latest/department-of-defense-defense-innovation-unit-announce-polygraph-effort-to\"> two companies to build prototypes\u003c/a>: Presage Technologies, which claims to be able to measure heart rate and breathing rate using standard cameras, and Altec Research, a medical sensor company now branching out into non-contact sensing technologies. A \u003ca href=\"https://www.diu.mil/latest/department-of-defense-defense-innovation-unit-announce-polygraph-effort-to\">screenshot\u003c/a> of Altec’s prototype technology released by the DIU shows that it tracks head movement, facial skin temperature, and pore activity. Presage Technologies and Altec Research did not respond to requests for comment. The DIU declined to comment.&nbsp;\u003c/p> \u003cdiv id='piano__post_body-mobile-1' class='piano__post_body'>\u003c/div>\n\u003cdiv class=\"wp-block-image\"> \u003cfigure class=\"wp-block-image size-full\">\u003cimg src=\"https://wp.technologyreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Altec_Poly_2.jpeg\" alt=\"Altec Research has built a prototype that tracks head movement, facial skin temperature and pore activity. \" class=\"wp-image-1145147\"/>\u003cfigcaption class=\"wp-element-caption\">Altec Research has built a prototype that tracks head movement, facial skin temperature, and pore activity. \u003c/figcaption>\u003cdiv class=\"image-credit\">ALTEC RESEARCH\u003c/div> \u003c/figure> \u003c/div> \u003cp>Current lie detection technology has barely changed since the polygraph was \u003ca href=\"https://www.wired.com/story/lie-detector-never-very-good-at-telling-truth/\">invented in the 1920s\u003c/a>. Examiners rely on blood pressure, pulse, breathing, and sweat measurements to determine if someone is lying. They make judgments about the veracity of respondents’ replies on the basis of differences in their physiological response to baseline questions like “Is the sky blue?” and target questions like “Have you ever committed a crime?”\u003c/p>  \u003cp>The federal government conducts tens of thousands of the tests each year while screening employees, but the reliability of this technology has been repeatedly challenged—and its results are rarely admissible in court. In 1983, Congress’s Office of Technology Assessment \u003ca href=\"https://liedetectortest.com/legal/1988-ota-report-congress-challenges-polygraph-science\">concluded\u003c/a> that there was very limited evidence supporting the polygraph’s use for screening employees, and in \u003ca href=\"https://irp.fas.org/congress/2003_hr/090403fienberg.html\">2003\u003c/a>, the US National Research Council (NRC) said evidence for its efficacy was “weak at best.”&nbsp;\u003c/p>  \u003cp>\u003ca href=\"https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16859438/\">Research\u003c/a> suggests humans can spot a lie just over half the time without any technical assistance. The American Polygraph Association \u003ca href=\"https://www.polygraph.org/polygraph_validity_research.php\">claims\u003c/a> the polygraph is between 80% and 94% accurate. But the 2003 NRC report pointed out that a screening test with this level of accuracy could still lead to a lot of mistakes. The DOD employs 2.8 million people; an imperfect system applied at that scale could end up falsely accusing tens of thousands.\u003c/p>  \u003cp>There are other issues too. Polygraph interpretations are often subjective: \u003ca href=\"https://www.wired.com/story/inside-polygraph-job-screening-black-mirror/\">Different examiners get wildly different results\u003c/a>, and people from minority groups are more likely to be judged as deceptive. What’s more, with training it’s possible for interviewees to learn a variety of countermeasures that can help beat the test; for example, they may artificially heighten their physiological response to baseline questions by stepping on a pin hidden in their shoe.&nbsp;\u003c/p> "},"children":[],"componentGroups":{"default":[]}},{"name":"mittr-plugin-extension/ad-unit-post-content","config":{"adUnit":"__site/__gutenberg-block-mobile","index":2,"shouldLoad":true,"sizes":[[300,250]],"sizeMapping":[],"displayScreen":"mobile"},"children":[],"componentGroups":{"default":[]}},{"name":"html","config":{"content":" \u003cp>“If you know how it works, you can beat it,” says Sophie van der Zee, an associate professor who studies deception at Erasmus University in Rotterdam. She says the machine’s biggest effect is deterrence—often, subjects confess before it even begins. “But that only works if people think a polygraph works,” she points out.\u003c/p> "},"children":[],"componentGroups":{"default":[]}},{"name":"mittr-plugin-extension/related","config":{"postID":"1140927","isPopular":true,"isAuto":true,"url":"https://www.technologyreview.com/2026/07/30/1140927/a-fundamental-flaw-leaves-llms-vulnerable-to-attack/","headline":"A fundamental flaw leaves LLMs strikingly vulnerable to attack","featuredImg":{"name":"image","config":{"aspectRatio":0.5625,"id":1140900,"alt":"chain links with one link is glowing green with a common phrase used to hack LLMs","caption":"","crops":[],"height":0,"imageSize":"related_story_thumbnail","lazyload":"1","lqipSrc":"https://wp.technologyreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/chain-link.jpg?quality=60&resize=60,33","postId":0,"retina":"1","showCaption":false,"sources":[{"transforms":{"fit":[212,9999]},"descriptor":212,"default":true}],"sourceTags":[],"src":"https://wp.technologyreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/chain-link.jpg","srcset":"https://wp.technologyreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/chain-link.jpg?fit=424,19998 424w,https://wp.technologyreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/chain-link.jpg?fit=212,9999 212w","url":"https://wp.technologyreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/chain-link.jpg","useBasicImg":false,"usingDataFallback":false,"width":0,"picture":false,"sizes":"212px","smartCropPosition":[50,50],"smartCropRatio":"56.25%"},"children":[],"componentGroups":{"default":[]}}},"children":[],"componentGroups":{"default":[]}},{"name":"html","config":{"content":" \u003cp>Various new strategies for lie detection have been attempted \u003ca href=\"https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2019/sep/05/the-race-to-create-a-perfect-lie-detector-and-the-dangers-of-succeeding\">over the decades\u003c/a>, with technologies ranging from thermal cameras to pupil trackers to brain scans. None of them have yielded reliable results outside the lab. The problem is that there’s no single telltale sign of lying that’s true for everyone all the time. “There is still no Pinocchio’s nose,” says van der Zee.&nbsp;\u003c/p>  \u003cp>AI could theoretically \u003ca href=\"https://www.technologyreview.com/2024/07/05/1094703/ai-lie-detectors-are-better-than-humans-at-spotting-lies/\">improve polygraphs\u003c/a> if it could find patterns in the data that examiners can’t. AI algorithms are also more likely to be used for “multi-modal” deception detection, which seeks to combine multiple measurements into an overall deception “score” that is harder for people to game. Three things are happening under the surface that lie detection tries to home in on, van der Zee says: physiological stress, cognitive load, and the conscious efforts people make to conceal the fact that they’re lying. Current polygraph technology tackles only one.\u003cbr>\u003cbr>“The more you can have combined methods that approach it from these three different angles, the more successful you will be,” van der Zee says. This isn’t a new concept—in the 2000s, researchers at Manchester Metropolitan University in the UK developed a system called \u003ca href=\"https://www.mmu.ac.uk/news-and-events/news/story/intelligent-lie-detector\">Silent Talker\u003c/a> that generated a deception score from video footage. This was later folded into iBorderCtrl, an EU-funded pilot program. In the US, a project called AVATAR incorporated eye tracking, voice analysis, and body movement detection into a tool for use at border crossings. All these projects have quietly faded away.&nbsp;\u003c/p>  \u003cp>Kotsoglou says combining AI and the polygraph is “the worst of both worlds” because it adds uncertainty on top of invalidity. Even if AI or machine learning can spot previously unseen patterns in physiological data, it won’t be able to reliably link them to lying because there is no real ground truth.&nbsp;\u003c/p>  \u003cp>“Even if you have all the records in the world from polygraph tests, you don't know whether those polygraph tests are right or not,” says Marion Oswald, a professor of law who has written with Kotsoglou on the use of polygraphs in the justice system. She fears that new forms of lie detection will, like the polygraph, be used more as a psychological prop than a scientific tool.&nbsp;\u003c/p>  \u003cp>“It seems very much a response to the concern of the current administration to leaks and perceived lack of loyalty,” says Oswald. “[Lie detection is] being used as a threat, to intimidate and force people to confess to things, as opposed to anything that's actually getting valid information.”\u003c/p> contentArticleHeader__secondDots--8b6f337a88e6067ec820cddee7df8b36"><div class="dotGrid__dots--cf24d0e6aff1f112b1e5d9065c4a71c1 dotGrid__blue--acac301fee94f7da075099d6526b2d56"></div></div><div class="contentArticleHeader__dots--f18af8845502d6a24e12e1c5a6d4683d contentArticleHeader__secondDots--8b6f337a88e6067ec820cddee7df8b36" style="background-image:radial-gradient(
                circle at 2px 2px,
                #BBC7E199
                2px,
                transparent 0
              )"></div></header></div><div class="columnArea--fullStory__wrapper--ccee5f31e66b5948da2a7c721aad125d columnArea__wrapper columnArea--fullStory__isStandard--6ae6bc9cb34f786f51175e8f697bd543"><div class="columnArea--fullStory__main--69d9dff03dc838997ac3b349fb620185"><div class="contentArea__wrapper--38c966634c2da29792cafb832d80f475 content-area"><div class="contentBody__wrapper--d9d8f9bb44c188246f70afcdc827cc4f"><div class="contentBody__overlay--d693d7b10ac848641212320075aaf64a"></div><div class="contentBody__content--42a60b56e419a26d9c3638a9dab52f55" id="content--body"><div><div class=""><div class="gutenbergContent__content--109b03a769a11e8ae3acbab352a64269 chronoton/executive-summary_0"><div class="chronotonExecutiveSummary__summaryContainer--3bc10da0658ecd8e2ef22c6023461fb5"><button class="chronotonExecutiveSummary__toggleButton--1cd6118db37e8a8252fc4cd8bbadcb85" aria-label="Collapse executive summary" aria-expanded="true" aria-controls="executive-summary-content" type="button"><span class="chronotonExecutiveSummary__toggleText--a713e14989fe65c5162db2b69cb422c9">EXECUTIVE SUMMARY</span><svg class="chronotonExecutiveSummary__toggleArrow--a8c1be9c06a9f066a767b3af80d859a1" width="11" height="7" viewBox="0 0 11 7" fill="none" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M1 1L5.5 5.5L10 1" stroke="#58C0B3" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-linecap="round"></path></svg></button></div></div><div><div class="gutenbergContent__content--109b03a769a11e8ae3acbab352a64269 html_1 html_first"> <p>The US government wants to spend $30.3 million over the next five years on an improved form of lie detector, according to a <a href="https://comptroller.war.gov/Portals/45/Documents/defbudget/FY2027/budget_justification/pdfs/03_RDT_and_E/RDTE_DCSA_PB_2027.pdf#page=53">Department of Defense budget request</a>. The program, called Polygraph+ or Polygraph Next, will focus on scoring algorithms that use artificial intelligence and machine learning and on a technique called “standoff sensing,” which refers to the ability to take physiological readings without attaching a device to a subject’s person.</p>  <p>According to details of the budget document, which were first reported by <a href="https://insidedefense.com/daily-news/pentagon-advances-polygraph-next-amid-extraordinary-joint-staff-leak-probe"><em>Inside Defense</em></a>, the project will “modernize federal polygraph and credibility assessment technologies” to improve their accuracy and reliability. But the project may be just the latest in a long line of failed attempts to use technology to detect lies. “It’s a misguided effort to reduce the complex to something that is tangible,” says Kyri Kotsoglou, a legal scholar at Northumbria University in the UK who studies the use of polygraphs in the justice system.</p> </div></div><div><div class="gutenbergContent__content--109b03a769a11e8ae3acbab352a64269 html_3"> <p>The move comes at a time of high tension within the department. Under Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, the Pentagon has been increasingly turning to polygraph tests in an attempt to find the sources of alleged leaks to the press. In September, the <em>New York Times</em> reported that <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/04/us/politics/pentagon-staff-polygraph-tests.html">around 50 officers</a> on the Joint Staff had been given polygraph tests after news coverage reported on the depletion of US weapons stockpiles in the war with Iran. </p>  <p>Polygraph+ will be run by the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency (DCSA), which conducts background checks for the federal government. According to the budget document, which has not yet been approved by Congress, the new technology will be used for vetting of prospective employees and “insider threat detection.” It is not yet clear which specific technologies will be used, and the DCSA did not respond to a request for more information. </p> <div id="piano__post_body-desktop-1" class="piano__post_body"></div>
 <p>But other Pentagon efforts offer potential clues. In 2023, the department’s Defense Innovation Unit (DIU) ran an open submission process to find companies with products that could be used for deception detection.</p>  <p>It selected<a href="https://www.diu.mil/latest/department-of-defense-defense-innovation-unit-announce-polygraph-effort-to"> two companies to build prototypes</a>: Presage Technologies, which claims to be able to measure heart rate and breathing rate using standard cameras, and Altec Research, a medical sensor company now branching out into non-contact sensing technologies. A <a href="https://www.diu.mil/latest/department-of-defense-defense-innovation-unit-announce-polygraph-effort-to">screenshot</a> of Altec’s prototype technology released by the DIU shows that it tracks head movement, facial skin temperature, and pore activity. Presage Technologies and Altec Research did not respond to requests for comment. The DIU declined to comment. </p> <div id="piano__post_body-mobile-1" class="piano__post_body"></div>
<div class="wp-block-image"> <figure class="wp-block-image size-full"><img src="https://wp.technologyreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Altec_Poly_2.jpeg" alt="Altec Research has built a prototype that tracks head movement, facial skin temperature and pore activity. " class="wp-image-1145147" /><figcaption class="wp-element-caption">Altec Research has built a prototype that tracks head movement, facial skin temperature, and pore activity. </figcaption><div class="image-credit">ALTEC RESEARCH</div> </figure> </div> <p>Current lie detection technology has barely changed since the polygraph was <a href="https://www.wired.com/story/lie-detector-never-very-good-at-telling-truth/">invented in the 1920s</a>. Examiners rely on blood pressure, pulse, breathing, and sweat measurements to determine if someone is lying. They make judgments about the veracity of respondents’ replies on the basis of differences in their physiological response to baseline questions like “Is the sky blue?” and target questions like “Have you ever committed a crime?”</p>  <p>The federal government conducts tens of thousands of the tests each year while screening employees, but the reliability of this technology has been repeatedly challenged—and its results are rarely admissible in court. In 1983, Congress’s Office of Technology Assessment <a href="https://liedetectortest.com/legal/1988-ota-report-congress-challenges-polygraph-science">concluded</a> that there was very limited evidence supporting the polygraph’s use for screening employees, and in <a href="https://irp.fas.org/congress/2003_hr/090403fienberg.html">2003</a>, the US National Research Council (NRC) said evidence for its efficacy was “weak at best.” </p>  <p><a href="https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16859438/">Research</a> suggests humans can spot a lie just over half the time without any technical assistance. The American Polygraph Association <a href="https://www.polygraph.org/polygraph_validity_research.php">claims</a> the polygraph is between 80% and 94% accurate. But the 2003 NRC report pointed out that a screening test with this level of accuracy could still lead to a lot of mistakes. The DOD employs 2.8 million people; an imperfect system applied at that scale could end up falsely accusing tens of thousands.</p>  <p>There are other issues too. Polygraph interpretations are often subjective: <a href="https://www.wired.com/story/inside-polygraph-job-screening-black-mirror/">Different examiners get wildly different results</a>, and people from minority groups are more likely to be judged as deceptive. What’s more, with training it’s possible for interviewees to learn a variety of countermeasures that can help beat the test; for example, they may artificially heighten their physiological response to baseline questions by stepping on a pin hidden in their shoe. </p> </div></div><div><div class="gutenbergContent__content--109b03a769a11e8ae3acbab352a64269 html_5"> <p>“If you know how it works, you can beat it,” says Sophie van der Zee, an associate professor who studies deception at Erasmus University in Rotterdam. She says the machine’s biggest effect is deterrence—often, subjects confess before it even begins. “But that only works if people think a polygraph works,” she points out.</p> </div></div><aside aria-label="Related Story - A fundamental flaw leaves LLMs strikingly vulnerable to attack" class="related__wrap"><h2 class="related__header">Related Story</h2><div class="related__content-wrap"><a aria-hidden="true" href="https://www.technologyreview.com/2026/07/30/1140927/a-fundamental-flaw-leaves-llms-vulnerable-to-attack/" class="related__featuredImg--link" tabindex="-1"><span class="image__wrapper--373a87c0cefdc42b3a8bd26457571412 image__aspectRatio--2c451d3b5ec4f1d8596af281c3c757bb" style="padding-bottom:56.25%"><span class=" lazy-load-image-background opacity" style="color:transparent;display:inline-block"><span class="image__img--e1a73f503bf0f4a3d2504e1d64ea29cb imgLazyLoaded" style="display:inline-block;object-position:50% 50%"></span></span></span><figcaption class="image__meta--16eb0f8dde685315ba1d77ae67c89391"></figcaption></a><a href="https://www.technologyreview.com/2026/07/30/1140927/a-fundamental-flaw-leaves-llms-vulnerable-to-attack/" class="related__link"><div class="">A fundamental flaw leaves LLMs strikingly vulnerable to attack</div></a><a href="https://www.technologyreview.com/2026/07/30/1140927/a-fundamental-flaw-leaves-llms-vulnerable-to-attack/" class="related__button button__wrapper--20b97b227471b3dd002defc980e6f965 button__primary--491aa0c640a989ad473fb309ceadf5d1">Read next</a></div></aside><div><div class="gutenbergContent__content--109b03a769a11e8ae3acbab352a64269 html_7"><p>Various new strategies for lie detection have been attempted <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2019/sep/05/the-race-to-create-a-perfect-lie-detector-and-the-dangers-of-succeeding">over the decades</a>, with technologies ranging from thermal cameras to pupil trackers to brain scans. None of them have yielded reliable results outside the lab. The problem is that there’s no single telltale sign of lying that’s true for everyone all the time. “There is still no Pinocchio’s nose,” says van der Zee. </p>  <p>AI could theoretically <a href="https://www.technologyreview.com/2024/07/05/1094703/ai-lie-detectors-are-better-than-humans-at-spotting-lies/">improve polygraphs</a> if it could find patterns in the data that examiners can’t. AI algorithms are also more likely to be used for “multi-modal” deception detection, which seeks to combine multiple measurements into an overall deception “score” that is harder for people to game. Three things are happening under the surface that lie detection tries to home in on, van der Zee says: physiological stress, cognitive load, and the conscious efforts people make to conceal the fact that they’re lying. Current polygraph technology tackles only one.<br /><br />“The more you can have combined methods that approach it from these three different angles, the more successful you will be,” van der Zee says. This isn’t a new concept—in the 2000s, researchers at Manchester Metropolitan University in the UK developed a system called <a href="https://www.mmu.ac.uk/news-and-events/news/story/intelligent-lie-detector">Silent Talker</a> that generated a deception score from video footage. This was later folded into iBorderCtrl, an EU-funded pilot program. In the US, a project called AVATAR incorporated eye tracking, voice analysis, and body movement detection into a tool for use at border crossings. All these projects have quietly faded away. </p>  <p>Kotsoglou says combining AI and the polygraph is “the worst of both worlds” because it adds uncertainty on top of invalidity. Even if AI or machine learning can spot previously unseen patterns in physiological data, it won’t be able to reliably link them to lying because there is no real ground truth. </p>  <p>“Even if you have all the records in the world from polygraph tests, you don't know whether those polygraph tests are right or not,” says Marion Oswald, a professor of law who has written with Kotsoglou on the use of polygraphs in the justice system. She fears that new forms of lie detection will, like the polygraph, be used more as a psychological prop than a scientific tool. </p>  <p>“It seems very much a response to the concern of the current administration to leaks and perceived lack of loyalty,” says Oswald. “[Lie detection is] being used as a threat, to intimidate and force people to confess to things, as opposed to anything that's actually getting valid information.”<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 1091.84 1091.84" class="monogramTLogo" aria-hidden="true"><polygon fill="#6d6e71" points="363.95 0 363.95 0 363.95 363.95 363.95 363.95 0 0 0"></polygon></svg> </p></div></div></div></div></div></div><footer class="contentFooter__wrapper--668cb9dffd30ed781105d3c21d83e9c4"><div         <item>
            <title><![CDATA[gpt-oss-safeguard technical report]]></title>
            <description><![CDATA[gpt-oss-safeguard-120b and gpt-oss-safeguard-20b are two open-weight reasoning models post-trained from the gpt-oss models and trained to reason from a provided policy in order to label content under that policy. In this report, we describe gpt-oss-safeguard’s capabilities and provide our baseline safety evaluations on the gpt-oss-safeguard models, using the underlying gpt-oss models as a baseline. For more information about the development and architecture of the underlying gpt-oss models, see the original gpt-oss model model card⁠.]]></description>

        <item>
            <title><![CDATA[Video generation models as world simulators]]></title>
            <description><![CDATA[We explore large-scale training of generative models on video data. Specifically, we train text-conditional diffusion models jointly on videos and images of variable durations, resolutions and aspect ratios. We leverage a transformer architecture that operates on spacetime patches of video and image latent codes. Our largest model, Sora, is capable of generating a minute of high fidelity video. Our results suggest that scaling video generation models is a promising path towards building general purpose simulators of the physical world.]]></description>
            <link>https://openai.com/index/video-generation-models-as-world-simulators</link>
            <guid isPermaLink="true">https://openai.com/index/video-generation-models-as-world-simulators</guid>
            <category><![CDATA[Research]]></category>
            <pubDate>Thu, 15 Feb 2024 08:00:00 GMT</pubDate>
        </item>

        <item>
            <title><![CDATA[Building an early warning system for LLM-aided biological threat creation]]></title>
            <description><![CDATA[We’re developing a blueprint for evaluating the risk that a large language model (LLM) could aid someone in creating a biological threat. In an evaluation involving both biology experts and students, we found that GPT-4 provides at most a mild uplift in biological threat creation accuracy. While this uplift is not large enough to be conclusive, our finding is a starting point for continued research and community deliberation. ]]></description>
            <link>https://openai.com/index/building-an-early-warning-system-for-llm-aided-biological-threat-creation</link>
            <guid isPermaLink="true">https://openai.com/index/building-an-early-warning-system-for-llm-aided-biological-threat-creation</guid>

        <item>
            <title><![CDATA[Improving mathematical reasoning with process supervision]]></title>
            <description><![CDATA[We’ve trained a model to achieve a new state-of-the-art in mathematical problem solving by rewarding each correct step of reasoning (“process supervision”) instead of simply rewarding the correct final answer (“outcome supervision”). In addition to boosting performance relative to outcome supervision, process supervision also has an important alignment benefit: it directly trains the model to produce a chain-of-thought that is endorsed by humans.]]></description>
            <link>https://openai.com/index/improving-mathematical-reasoning-with-process-supervision</link>
            <guid isPermaLink="true">https://openai.com/index/improving-mathematical-reasoning-with-process-supervision</guid>

        <item>
            <title><![CDATA[Forecasting potential misuses of language models for disinformation campaigns and how to reduce risk]]></title>
            <description><![CDATA[OpenAI researchers collaborated with Georgetown University’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology and the Stanford Internet Observatory to investigate how large language models might be misused for disinformation purposes. The collaboration included an October 2021 workshop bringing together 30 disinformation researchers, machine learning experts, and policy analysts, and culminated in a co-authored report building on more than a year of research. This report outlines the threats that language models pose to the information environment if used to augment disinformation campaigns and introduces a framework for analyzing potential mitigations. Read the full report here.]]></description>
            <link>https://openai.com/index/forecasting-misuse</link>
            <guid isPermaLink="true">https://openai.com/index/forecasting-misuse</guid>
            <category><![CDATA[Safety & Alignment]]></category>
            <pubDate>Wed, 11 Jan 2023 08:00:00 GMT</pubDate>

            <description><![CDATA[As part of our DALL·E 2 research preview, more than 3,000 artists from more than 118 countries have incorporated DALL·E into their creative workflows. The artists in our early access group have helped us discover new uses for DALL·E and have served as key voices as we’ve made decisions about DALL·E’s features.]]></description>

        <item>

            <description><![CDATA[In order to share the magic of DALL·E 2 with a broad audience, we needed to reduce the risks associated with powerful image generation models. To this end, we put various guardrails in place to prevent generated images from violating our content policy.]]></description>
            <link>https://openai.com/index/dall-e-2-pre-training-mitigations</link>

        <item>
            <title><![CDATA[Learning to play Minecraft with Video PreTraining]]></title>
            <description><![CDATA[We trained a neural network to play Minecraft by Video PreTraining (VPT) on a massive unlabeled video dataset of human Minecraft play, while using only a small amount of labeled contractor data. With fine-tuning, our model can learn to craft diamond tools, a task that usually takes proficient humans over 20 minutes (24,000 actions). Our model uses the native human interface of keypresses and mouse movements, making it quite general, and represents a step towards general computer-using agents.]]></description>
            <link>https://openai.com/index/vpt</link>
            <guid isPermaLink="true">https://openai.com/index/vpt</guid>
            <category><![CDATA[Research]]></category>
            <pubDate>Thu, 23 Jun 2022 07:00:00 GMT</pubDate>
        </item>

        <item>
            <title><![CDATA[AI-written critiques help humans notice flaws]]></title>
            <description><![CDATA[We trained “critique-writing” models to describe flaws in summaries. Human evaluators find flaws in summaries much more often when shown our model’s critiques. Larger models are better at self-critiquing, with scale improving critique-writing more than summary-writing. This shows promise for using AI systems to assist human supervision of AI systems on difficult tasks.]]></description>
            <link>https://openai.com/index/critiques</link>
            <guid isPermaLink="true">https://openai.com/index/critiques</guid>
            <category><![CDATA[Safety & Alignment]]></category>
            <pubDate>Mon, 13 Jun 2022 07:00:00 GMT</pubDate>
        </item>

        <item>
            <title><![CDATA[Multimodal neurons in artificial neural networks]]></title>
            <description><![CDATA[We’ve discovered neurons in CLIP that respond to the same concept whether presented literally, symbolically, or conceptually. This may explain CLIP’s accuracy in classifying surprising visual renditions of concepts, and is also an important step toward understanding the associations and biases that CLIP and similar models learn.]]></description>
            <link>https://openai.com/index/multimodal-neurons</link>
            <guid isPermaLink="true">https://openai.com/index/multimodal-neurons</guid>
            <category><![CDATA[Research]]></category>
            <pubDate>Thu, 04 Mar 2021 08:00:00 GMT</pubDate>
        </item>

            <description><![CDATA[We’ve scaled Kubernetes clusters to 7,500 nodes, producing a scalable infrastructure for large models like GPT-3, CLIP, and DALL·E, but also for rapid small-scale iterative research such as Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models.]]></description>

        <item>
            <title><![CDATA[DALL·E: Creating images from text]]></title>
            <description><![CDATA[We’ve trained a neural network called DALL·E that creates images from text captions for a wide range of concepts expressible in natural language.]]></description>

        <item>
            <title><![CDATA[CLIP: Connecting text and images]]></title>
            <description><![CDATA[We’re introducing a neural network called CLIP which efficiently learns visual concepts from natural language supervision. CLIP can be applied to any visual classification benchmark by simply providing the names of the visual categories to be recognized, similar to the “zero-shot” capabilities of GPT-2 and GPT-3.]]></description>
            <link>https://openai.com/index/clip</link>
            <guid isPermaLink="true">https://openai.com/index/clip</guid>

        <item>
            <title><![CDATA[Image GPT]]></title>
            <description><![CDATA[We find that, just as a large transformer model trained on language can generate coherent text, the same exact model trained on pixel sequences can generate coherent image completions and samples. By establishing a correlation between sample quality and image classification accuracy, we show that our best generative model also contains features competitive with top convolutional nets in the unsupervised setting.]]></description>
            <link>https://openai.com/index/image-gpt</link>
            <guid isPermaLink="true">https://openai.com/index/image-gpt</guid>

        <item>
            <title><![CDATA[AI and efficiency]]></title>
            <description><![CDATA[We’re releasing an analysis showing that since 2012 the amount of compute needed to train a neural net to the same performance on ImageNet classification has been decreasing by a factor of 2 every 16 months. Compared to 2012, it now takes 44 times less compute to train a neural network to the level of AlexNet (by contrast, Moore’s Law would yield an 11x cost improvement over this period). Our results suggest that for AI tasks with high levels of recent investment, algorithmic progress has yielded more gains than classical hardware efficiency.]]></description>
            <link>https://openai.com/index/ai-and-efficiency</link>
            <guid isPermaLink="true">https://openai.com/index/ai-and-efficiency</guid>
            <category><![CDATA[Research]]></category>
            <pubDate>Tue, 05 May 2020 07:00:00 GMT</pubDate>
        </item>
        <item>
            <title><![CDATA[Jukebox]]></title>
            <description><![CDATA[We’re introducing Jukebox, a neural net that generates music, including rudimentary singing, as raw audio in a variety of genres and artist styles. We’re releasing the model weights and code, along with a tool to explore the generated samples.]]></description>
            <link>https://openai.com/index/jukebox</link>
            <guid isPermaLink="true">https://openai.com/index/jukebox</guid>
            <category><![CDATA[Research]]></category>
            <pubDate>Thu, 30 Apr 2020 07:00:00 GMT</pubDate>
        </item>
        <item>
            <title><![CDATA[Improving verifiability in AI development]]></title>
            <description><![CDATA[We’ve contributed to a multi-stakeholder report by 58 co-authors at 30 organizations, including the Centre for the Future of Intelligence, Mila, Schwartz Reisman Institute for Technology and Society, Center for Advanced Study in the Behavioral Sciences, and Center for Security and Emerging Technologies. This report describes 10 mechanisms to improve the verifiability of claims made about AI systems. Developers can use these tools to provide evidence that AI systems are safe, secure, fair, or privacy-preserving. Users, policymakers, and civil society can use these tools to evaluate AI development processes.]]></description>
            <link>https://openai.com/index/improving-verifiability</link>
            <guid isPermaLink="true">https://openai.com/index/improving-verifiability</guid>
            <category><![CDATA[Research]]></category>
            <pubDate>Thu, 16 Apr 2020 07:00:00 GMT</pubDate>
        </item>
        <item>
            <title><![CDATA[OpenAI Microscope]]></title>
            <description><![CDATA[We’re introducing OpenAI Microscope, a collection of visualizations of every significant layer and neuron of eight vision “model organisms” which are often studied in interpretability. Microscope makes it easier to analyze the features that form inside these neural networks, and we hope it will help the research community as we move towards understanding these complicated systems.]]></description>
            <link>https://openai.com/index/microscope</link>
            <guid isPermaLink="true">https://openai.com/index/microscope</guid>
            <category><![CDATA[Research]]></category>

        <item>
            <title><![CDATA[Deep double descent]]></title>
            <description><![CDATA[We show that the double descent phenomenon occurs in CNNs, ResNets, and transformers: performance first improves, then gets worse, and then improves again with increasing model size, data size, or training time. This effect is often avoided through careful regularization. While this behavior appears to be fairly universal, we don’t yet fully understand why it happens, and view further study of this phenomenon as an important research direction.]]></description>
            <link>https://openai.com/index/deep-double-descent</link>
            <guid isPermaLink="true">https://openai.com/index/deep-double-descent</guid>
            <category><![CDATA[Research]]></category>
            <pubDate>Thu, 05 Dec 2019 08:00:00 GMT</pubDate>
        </item>

        <item>
            <title><![CDATA[GPT-2: 1.5B release]]></title>
            <description><![CDATA[As the final model release of GPT-2’s staged release, we’re releasing the largest version (1.5B parameters) of GPT-2 along with code and model weights to facilitate detection of outputs of GPT-2 models. While there have been larger language models released since August, we’ve continued with our original staged release plan in order to provide the community with a test case of a full staged release process. We hope that this test case will be useful to developers of future powerful models, and we’re actively continuing the conversation with the AI community on responsible publication.]]></description>
            <link>https://openai.com/index/gpt-2-1-5b-release</link>
            <guid isPermaLink="true">https://openai.com/index/gpt-2-1-5b-release</guid>
            <category><![CDATA[Research]]></category>

        </item>
        <item>
            <title><![CDATA[Solving Rubik’s Cube with a robot hand]]></title>
            <description><![CDATA[We’ve trained a pair of neural networks to solve the Rubik’s Cube with a human-like robot hand. The neural networks are trained entirely in simulation, using the same reinforcement learning code as OpenAI Five paired with a new technique called Automatic Domain Randomization (ADR). The system can handle situations it never saw during training, such as being prodded by a stuffed giraffe. This shows that reinforcement learning isn’t just a tool for virtual tasks, but can solve physical-world problems requiring unprecedented dexterity.]]></description>
            <link>https://openai.com/index/solving-rubiks-cube</link>
            <guid isPermaLink="true">https://openai.com/index/solving-rubiks-cube</guid>
            <category><![CDATA[Research]]></category>
            <pubDate>Tue, 15 Oct 2019 07:00:00 GMT</pubDate>
        </item>

            <description><![CDATA[We are now accepting applications for our third class of OpenAI Scholars.]]></description>
